content:
**Visual observations:**
- **Plant part**: Cross-section of a corn stalk (transverse cut)
- **Key features**:
  - Very dark, nearly black outer rind around the entire circumference of the cut stalk
  - White/cream-colored pith in the center
  - Wet/glistening appearance on the cut surface
  - Some yellowing visible in the pith center
  - Outer husk tissue is also dark brown/rotted

**Reasoning through candidates:**

- **Anthracnose_stalk_rot**: Classic diagnostic sign is shiny black discoloration of the outer rind. Cross-sections show this dark ring very clearly. Matches strongly.
- **Charcoal_stalk_rot**: Would show gray/silvery internal tissue with tiny black sclerotia (pepper-like dots) scattered throughout the pith — not matching.
- **Diplodia_stalk_rot**: Would show prominent white cottony mycelium filling the interior, brown discoloration — only partially matches.
- **Fusarium**: Would show pink/salmon-colored mycelium or staining — not visible here.
- **Bacterial_stalk_rot**: Wet, mushy, foul-smelling; the rind wouldn't turn this distinctly black.
- **Physoderma_stalk_rot**: Black rot specifically at nodes.

The **black, darkened outer rind** on the stalk cross-section is the hallmark diagnostic feature of **Anthracnose stalk rot** (*Colletotrichum graminicola*). The pattern here — dark ring around the periphery with relatively intact (though discolored) pith — is textbook for this disease.
